source_title: CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — Security Best Practices

cleaned_entries.title: Mandatory SecurityContext for all pods (CIS 5.2)
cleaned_entries.content:
Mandatory SecurityContext for all pods (CIS 5.2)

Every Pod must define a restrictive SecurityContext. Pod-level: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1001, runAsGroup: 1001, fsGroup: 1001, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Container-level: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: [ALL]. Mount emptyDir for /tmp if read-only filesystem is set.

Decision rules:
- Apply both pod-level and container-level SecurityContext — they are complementary
- Use seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault to restrict system calls
- Mount emptyDir volumes at paths that require write access (e.g. /tmp)

Trade-offs:
- readOnlyRootFilesystem may break applications that write to the container filesystem — identify and mount emptyDir for those paths

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying pods without any SecurityContext
- Setting allowPrivilegeEscalation: true or omitting it (defaults to true without explicit false)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS enforces Pod Security Standards — set namespace labels pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted

cleaned_entries.title: RBAC with least privilege (CIS 5.1)
cleaned_entries.content:
RBAC with least privilege (CIS 5.1)

Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per application with automountServiceAccountToken: false. Define a Role with only required verbs on required resources. Bind via RoleBinding. Do not grant access to secrets unless strictly necessary.

Decision rules:
- Create a dedicated ServiceAccount for each workload — never use the default ServiceAccount
- Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on ServiceAccount to prevent token auto-mounting
- Grant only required verbs (get, list) on required resources — never use wildcard (*)

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained RBAC requires understanding of which API resources each workload actually accesses

Anti-patterns:
- Using the default ServiceAccount for application workloads
- Granting cluster-admin or wildcard permissions to application ServiceAccounts
- Adding secrets to the Role resource list without justification

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to EKS IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for AWS API access from pods

cleaned_entries.title: Network isolation with default-deny NetworkPolicy (CIS 5.3)
cleaned_entries.content:
Network isolation with default-deny NetworkPolicy (CIS 5.3)

Apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy in each namespace (podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]). Then add explicit allow policies per service. Example: allow Ingress from ingress-nginx namespace on port 8000 only for pods matching app=api.

Decision rules:
- Start with a default-deny-all policy in every namespace
- Add explicit ingress and egress allow rules only for required traffic paths
- Use namespaceSelector for cross-namespace traffic (e.g. allowing ingress controller)

Trade-offs:
- NetworkPolicy requires a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave) — does not work with Flannel alone

Anti-patterns:
- Operating namespaces with no NetworkPolicy (all traffic allowed by default)
- Using podSelector: {} in allow policies without scoping by policyTypes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use VPC CNI with Calico on EKS for NetworkPolicy enforcement
- Complement with Security Groups for Pods on EKS for L4 controls

cleaned_entries.title: Secrets management with External Secrets Operator (CIS 5.4)
cleaned_entries.content:
Secrets management with External Secrets Operator (CIS 5.4)

Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) or Sealed Secrets instead of plain Kubernetes Secret manifests. ESO ExternalSecret references a SecretStore (e.g. vault-backend) and syncs secrets into a Kubernetes Secret. ConfigMaps should hold only non-sensitive configuration.

Decision rules:
- Never commit plain Kubernetes Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to version control
- Use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, or GCP Secret Manager
- Use ConfigMaps exclusively for non-sensitive configuration (APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL)

Trade-offs:
- ESO adds operational complexity — requires installing the controller and configuring SecretStore
- Sealed Secrets is simpler but less flexible — secrets can only be decrypted by the cluster

Anti-patterns:
- Storing database URLs or passwords in ConfigMaps (not encrypted at rest)
- Committing Kubernetes Secrets with real credentials to git repositories

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use ESO with AWS Secrets Manager provider on EKS
- Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative

cleaned_entries.title: Mandatory resource requests and limits (CIS 5.2.4)
cleaned_entries.content:
Mandatory resource requests and limits (CIS 5.2.4)

Every container must define both resources.requests and resources.limits. Example: requests memory 128Mi cpu 100m, limits memory 512Mi cpu 500m. Without limits, a single pod can starve other workloads on the node.

Decision rules:
- Define both requests (scheduler hint) and limits (enforcement) for every container
- Use LimitRange objects to enforce defaults for namespaces missing explicit resource declarations

Trade-offs:
- Limits that are too tight cause OOMKilled events or CPU throttling — profile workloads before setting values

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying containers with no resource limits to shared cluster nodes
- Setting limits without requests — scheduler cannot make optimal placement decisions

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS node autoscaling (Karpenter) uses requests to pack pods onto nodes efficiently

cleaned_entries.title: Liveness and Readiness probes for workload health
cleaned_entries.content:
Liveness and Readiness probes for workload health

Define livenessProbe (restarts unhealthy pods: httpGet /health, initialDelaySeconds 15, periodSeconds 20, failureThreshold 3) and readinessProbe (removes unhealthy pods from Service endpoints: httpGet /ready, initialDelaySeconds 5, periodSeconds 10) for every container.

Decision rules:
- Use readinessProbe to control traffic routing — pod is only added to Service endpoints when ready
- Use livenessProbe to restart pods stuck in an unrecoverable state
- Set startupProbe for slow-starting applications to prevent premature liveness failures

Trade-offs:
- Overly aggressive liveness probes (short timeouts, low failureThreshold) cause unnecessary restarts
- Missing readiness probes cause traffic to be sent to not-yet-ready pods

Anti-patterns:
- Using the same endpoint and thresholds for both liveness and readiness probes
- Not defining any health probes — Kubernetes cannot detect application-level failures

cleaned_entries.title: Pod Disruption Budget for high availability
cleaned_entries.content:
Pod Disruption Budget for high availability

A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions (node drains, rolling updates). Example: minAvailable: 2 with selector app=api ensures at least 2 pods remain available during node maintenance.

Decision rules:
- Create a PDB for every production Deployment with more than 1 replica
- Use minAvailable (absolute) or maxUnavailable (percentage) depending on SLO requirements

Trade-offs:
- PDB with minAvailable equal to replicas will block node drains — leave at least 1 pod drainable

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying multi-replica workloads without a PDB — all pods may be disrupted simultaneously
- Setting minAvailable: 0 — defeats the purpose of the PDB

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- PDB works with EKS Managed Node Groups during node version upgrades

cleaned_entries.title: Ingress with TLS termination
cleaned_entries.content:
Ingress with TLS termination

Configure Ingress with TLS using cert-manager (cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod). Annotations: ssl-redirect: true, force-ssl-redirect: true. TLS spec references a Secret containing the certificate. All HTTP traffic redirected to HTTPS at the ingress level.

Decision rules:
- Always terminate TLS at the Ingress — never expose plain HTTP to the internet
- Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated certificate provisioning and renewal
- Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: true to enforce HTTPS

Trade-offs:
- Let's Encrypt rate limits apply — use staging issuer for testing
- Certificate renewal requires outbound internet access from the cluster for ACME challenges

Anti-patterns:
- Exposing services over HTTP in production
- Using self-signed certificates without a trust chain (causes browser/client warnings)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Alternatively use AWS ALB Ingress Controller with ACM certificates on EKS
